say: Welcome to Math Inquirers P6! The PSLE is done, so there is no exam today: just puzzles, patterns and code.
Every lesson we notice a pattern, test it in code, and explain why. Today’s question: how can you find the 100th number in a pattern without writing out all 100?
Pairs. I will show a sequence card. Take your time and type the next two terms in the chat. If you spot the rule, say it. There is no race and there are no points.
Careful: not every card adds the same amount each time.

Pattern 1 is a triangle made of 3 matchsticks. Each new pattern adds one more triangle in the row. Before you build anything: how many sticks will pattern 100 need? Write your guess in the corner of your whiteboard.
stuck: Stuck building: lay the triangles point up, point down, point up, so each new triangle shares a stick.
Stuck on pattern 100: “How many sticks does each new triangle add? How many new triangles come after the first one?”

say: “5, 8, 11, 14. The term-to-term rule is add 3. That is great for the next term, but slow for the 100th: I would have to add 3 ninety-nine times.”

“Adding 3 each time is like the 3 times table: 3, 6, 9, 12. Each term is 2 more than the times-table number. So the nth term is 3 × n + 2, which we write 3n + 2. Check the 4th term: 3 × 4 + 2 = 14. Yes.”

“So the 100th term is 3 × 100 + 2 = 302. Now I test it in code. I set term to 5, the 1st term. From the 1st term to the 100th term there are 99 jumps, so repeat 99, change term by 3, then say term. It says 302. The maths and the code agree.”

do: Ask: “What is the difference? Which times table is it like?”
Ask: “Check your rule with the 1st term AND the 4th term. Does it work for both?”
Ask: “How many jumps are there from the 1st term to the 20th term?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Write the times table of the difference under the sequence.”
Hint 2: “How far is each term from the times-table number under it?”
Hint 3: “Count the jumps for a small case first: from the 1st term to the 4th term is 3 jumps.”

say: “Ali says the 100th term of 7, 10, 13, … is 7 + 3 × 100 = 307. Is he right?”
ask: “Ali says the 100th term of 7, 10, 13, … is 7 + 3 × 100 = 307. Is he right?”

No. The 1st term is already 7 before any jump, so the 100th term is only 99 jumps away: 7 + 3 × 99 = 304. The rule 3n + 4 gives 304 too. The rule is fastest for one far term; code is best for listing many terms or checking an answer.

say: “Today you found the 100th term without writing 100 numbers, and you tested it in code. That is what mathematicians and programmers both do.”
“Do the exit ticket on your own, then show me.”

p6l1-title.note: Objective: Continue a sequence, find the rule for the nth term of a sequence with a constant difference, use it to find far terms such as the 100th, work backwards to decide whether a number is in a sequence, and test predictions with a loop and a variable in Scratch. Materials: Laptop or desktop with Scratch 3 open (scratch.mit.edu, no account needed), about 25 matchsticks or toothpicks per child (or squared paper), mini whiteboard, workbook. Optional: a Python editor for children who already know Python. Online: The tutor shares the slides and a Scratch window. Share your Scratch window and build the four blocks together on screen; the blocks are also on the slide. Block colours on our slides are simplified; in Scratch, find blocks by the category name on the left, not by colour. Scratch is free at scratch.mit.edu and needs no account in class. Children tick their own work against the answer slide or share their screen when asked; nothing is held up to the camera. Matchsticks can be drawn as lines. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson, with a standing flex buffer): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6, warm-up 6 to 12.5, explore 12.5 to 25 (matchsticks first, then Scratch), mini-lesson 25 to 36 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 36 to 40.5, worksheet 40.5 to 74 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it (page 1 is the maths, page 2 is the code), flex 74 to 76.5 (unscripted: use it for Think harder or catch-up; it is lost first), talk time 76.5 to 81.5, exit slip 81.5 to 86, looking back 86 to 88, close and stamp 88 to 90. Python: the optional Python version of each program is in the notes of the code slides and in the workbook Python corner. SPINE: Today's tool is Spot the pattern. Find the rule, test it on a new case, then use it to jump far. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p6l1-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6. These are ideas we have not learnt yet: say so, and say that guessing and "I do not know" are welcome and nobody is marked. Read the two puzzles aloud. Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone can get a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle on today's idea. ONE check moment only: after both puzzles, everyone says the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Never private chat. Never compare answers across children, never read wrong answers aloud. Then click to reveal the answers one after the other and move on with no reaction round: say each answer in 15 words or fewer, then say: "Both of these are what we learn today." Answers: Puzzle 1: 9 sticks. Each new triangle adds 2 more sticks (3, 5, 7, 9). Any child can draw it and count. Puzzle 2: $43. Each km adds $2, so 2 × 20 + 3 = 43. (Not 2 × 20 = 40: the $3 start charge is there from the beginning.) A guess or “I do not know” is fine; we will learn how today. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: say "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Nobody is singled out. Any child can choose it and any child can go back. Never announce who is on which page and never say advanced or top group. Do not record this as a mark. Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

p6l1-warm1.note: Minutes 6 to 10. Pairs (online: type in the chat). No racing, no points. Show one card at a time by pointing; click to reveal its answer (clicks go card 1 to card 4; four cards only, so the warm-up fits its 6.5 minutes). Ask for the rule every time. Card 3 and card 4 are traps: the difference is NOT the same each time (square numbers go up by 3, 5, 7, 9; in card 4 each term is the sum of the two before, the Fibonacci numbers). Say: "Today we focus on the friendly kind, where the difference stays the same, like cards 1 and 2."

p6l1-warm2.note: Minutes 10 to 12.5. Thumbs or a whisper to a partner, then click to reveal. Three questions only. Q1 and Q2 are the seed of today: 2, 4, 6, 8 is the 2 times table, so the 10th term is 2 × 10 = 20. 3, 5, 7, 9 is always 1 more than the 2 times table, so the 10th term is 21. Ask: "How did you get Q2 without counting on?" Q3: 12 + 6 × 5 = 42 (6 weeks, 6 jumps of $5, because Ali starts with $12 before any saving).

p6l1-explore1.note: Minutes 12.5 to 25 (this slide 12.5 to 16.5). Pairs build with matchsticks (online: draw the sticks as lines). Insist on a written prediction for pattern 10 and pattern 100 BEFORE anything else. Scratch is NOT opened in this part: the loop that checks a pattern is built once, live, in the mini-lesson (the slide Test it in code), so nothing is built twice. Go further what-if (not a slide: paste it in the chat for any pair that finishes early, and take it up only if a pair wants to share): What if each shape in the row were a SQUARE, sharing one side with the next? Predict how many sticks 10 squares in a row need. Then test pattern 3 by drawing. Answer: 31 sticks. The first square uses 4 sticks and each new square adds 3: 4 + 3 × 9 = 31, or 3 × 10 + 1.

p6l1-explore2.note: Minutes 16.5 to 25. Pairs keep working, then gather. Two questions (pattern 10 is read from the table: 21). Answers: 1) 201: each new triangle adds 2 sticks, so 3 + 2 × 99 = 201; or "2 sticks per triangle plus 1 extra", 2 × 100 + 1 = 201. Both are right: celebrate both methods. 2) Pattern 37: work backwards, 75 − 1 = 74, 74 ÷ 2 = 37.

p6l1-teach1.note: Minutes 25 to 27. Teach. n means the position (1st, 2nd, 3rd …). Think-aloud: "Add 2 each time. That gets me the next term, but for the 50th I would add 2 forty-nine times. The difference is 2, so I write the 2 times table underneath (click). Every term is 5 more than the 2 times-table number (click). So the term in position n is 2 × n + 5. In algebra we write 2n + 5, the same letter idea you used for the PSLE." Check with n = 3: 2 × 3 + 5 = 11, which matches.

p6l1-we1.note: Minutes 27 to 29. Click to reveal each step, asking the group to predict it first. Stress step 3: always check the rule on a term you can see, not only the 1st. Think-aloud: "3n on its own would give 3, 6, 9, 12. Ours are 5, 8, 11, 14, always 2 more. So 3n + 2."

p6l1-try1.note: Minutes 29 to 30. Whiteboards. a) Compare with 5, 10, 15, 20: 1 less, so 5n − 1; 500 − 1 = 499. b) 2, 4, 6, 8: 8 more, so 2n + 8; 208. c) 7, 14, 21, 28: 6 less, so 7n − 6; 694. Check c with the 4th term: 28 − 6 = 22. Watch for children writing 7n + 1 (they added the 1st term instead of comparing).

p6l1-we2.note:
Minutes 30 to 34. This is the first time Scratch is opened today (about 4 minutes): open scratch.mit.edu, click Create, and build it live while children copy (make a variable called term first: Variables, Make a Variable). Ask before step 3: "How many times should it repeat?" Many say 100. Draw 4 terms with 3 jumps between them on the whiteboard: 4 terms, 3 jumps. So 100 terms, 99 jumps. Run it: 302. Then try repeat 100: it says 305, the 101st term. Python version (optional):
term = 5
for i in range(99):
 term = term + 3
print(term)
It prints 302.

p6l1-key.note: Minutes 34 to 36. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Using only the difference as the rule (writing 3n for 5, 8, 11, …) and not comparing with the 1st term. (2) Off by one: doing 100 jumps from the 1st term (5 + 3 × 100) instead of 99, in the maths and in the repeat block. (3) Putting "change" before "say" in a loop, so the sprite never says the 1st term.

p6l1-break.note: Minutes 36 to 40.5. 4.5 minutes, away from the keyboard. Answers: the pattern repeats every 3 moves. 20 = 6 × 3 + 2, so the 20th move is the 2nd in its group: clap. 30 = 10 × 3, so the 30th move ends a group: stomp.

p6l1-teachwhich.note: Minutes 40.5 to 43. Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q1d and Q3). This is the PSLE "think of a number" idea run backwards: undo the − 1, then undo the × 3. Check step 1 forwards: 3 × 21 − 1 = 62. For step 2, ask: "Which terms are near 100?" (98 is the 33rd, 101 would need n = 33⅔.)

p6l1-trywhich.note: Minutes 43 to 46. Whiteboards. a) Rule 4n − 2: 4n = 52, n = 13. b) Rule 5n + 1: 5n = 95, n = 19. c) Rule 4n: every term is a multiple of 4, so every term is even; 75 is odd.

p6l1-ws1.note: Minutes 46 to 58. Pairs talk before they write. Ask "How did you check your rule?" Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Children who finish early test Q2 in Scratch: set term to the 1st term, repeat 99, change term by the difference, say term.

p6l1-ws1ans.note: Minutes 58 to 60.5. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q2 (the rule idea), about 35 seconds a question. Q1a: 4 sticks for the first square, then only 3 for each new square because it shares a side. Q2: the other two sequences (2n + 7 and 0.5n) are now on the Think harder page. Q3b: 4n + 1 = 101, 4n = 100, n = 25.

p6l1-teachtrace.note:
Minutes 60.5 to 63. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4, and the Q6 bug hunt as the second panel). Point at each block in order and say what the computer does: "x is 1. Loop 1: change x by 4, x is 5, say 5." Click a row after children say it. Then ask for repeat 50 WITHOUT tracing 50 rows: x starts at 1 and gets 50 jumps of 4. Python (optional):
x = 1
for i in range(3):
 x = x + 4
 print(x)
Prints 5, 9, 13. Bug hunt (Q6), the fence-post idea: 5 posts have 4 gaps, so the 1st term is there before any jump. Ben wants the 20th term of 2, 6, 10, … and writes repeat 20: it says 82, but the rule 4n − 2 gives 78. 1st term to 20th term is 19 jumps (2 + 19 × 4 = 78). Is there another fix? Yes: start n at −2 and keep repeat 20.

p6l1-ws2.note: Minutes 63 to 71. Children work alone on Q4 and Q6; Q5 (plan the code) is the take-home question, marked with a star in the workbook. Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Let them test Q4 and Q6 in Scratch AFTER writing their prediction. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson.

p6l1-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71 to 74. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q6 (repeat 49, the fence-post idea). Q5 is the take-home question: the answer is here so children can mark it at home, and you take it up at the start of the next lesson. Say must come before change. The last number said is the 20th term, 6 × 20 − 2 = 118 (n ends at 124 but it is never said). Q6: 3 + 50 × 4 = 203 is the 51st term.

p6l1-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Answers: 1) 7: go back 4 jumps of 4 from 23 (23 − 16 = 7); rule 4n + 3. 2) 4: from the 1st to the 10th term is 9 jumps, and 36 ÷ 9 = 4 (rule 4n). 3) 10, 20, 30, 40, … (rule 10n): 99 jumps must add 990, so each jump is 10.

p6l1-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then the "see it" slide, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) 14, 29, 44 and 59. 2) 15 (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5); with repeat 100 it says 5050.

p6l1-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? Q1: what are the next marks on each line? Q2: what happens to k and to t in the first loop?

p6l1-chwalk.note:
Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. Q1: the common terms go up by 15 because 15 is the smallest number in both the 3 and the 5 times tables; 14 + 15 = 29, then 44, then 59 (the next, 74, is too big). Q2: t adds up 1, 2, 3, … These are the triangle numbers. Python (optional):
t = 0
k = 0
for i in range(100):
 k = k + 1
 t = t + k
print(t)
Prints 5050.

p6l1-talk.note: Minutes 76.5 to 81.5. One question only. Pairs talk for 90 seconds, then volunteers share. Listen for: No. The 1st term is already 7 before any jump, so the 100th term is only 99 jumps away: 7 + 3 × 99 = 304. The rule 3n + 4 gives 304 too. Second question (only if flex is left, otherwise it is the opener of the next lesson): "When is the rule better than adding on? When is code better than both?" (The rule is fastest for one far term; code is best for listing many terms or checking.)

p6l1-exit.note: Minutes 81.5 to 86. Answers: (a) 3n + 5 (b) 305 (c) 99 times. Extension: make the program say the position and the term together (for example "term 7 is 23") using a second variable pos and the join block, then make it stop at the first term bigger than 1000 (the 333rd term, 1001).

p6l1-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 86 to 88. Start the timer (75 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.
